author: AnthropicAI
text:
Anthropic’s Economics team is sharing a new model of how AI might affect economic growth, jobs, wages, and more by 2030.

Explore the scenarios, tell us what you think will happen, and see how your answers compare to more than 10,000 Americans. https://t.co/AvQlEZNxR0

author: AnthropicAI
text:
The economic model breaks jobs down into bundles of tasks. AI can help someone complete a task faster or better, do the task itself, leave the task untouched, or create new tasks. 

Based on how you expect AI to affect tasks by 2030, our scenario explorer models AI’s potential impact on the US economy.

The scenario explorer focuses on three possible scenarios: modest, substantial, and extreme. The economy grows across all three scenarios. But in more transformative scenarios, AI automates more knowledge work, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are shared across society.

Like all economic models, ours simplifies a more complex reality. But by building better scenarios of our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure everyone benefits from it.

author: ANSPRASAD_TN
text:
The task-bundle frame is the right unit. Jobs are not atoms. AI can augment a task, automate it, leave it, or invent a new one. That is standard labor economics, and it is a cleaner starting point than “jobs in, jobs out.”

The published scenarios, at 2025 prices, are more specific than the post. Modest: US GDP about $34.1T in 2030, +1.6% versus a no-AI path, internet-scale. Substantial: $36.3T, +8.3%; AI can do roughly half of knowledge work, not all of it adopted. Extreme: $44.4T, +32.4%; growth near 15% a year, doubling about every 4.5 years, and it is described as likely needing recursively self-improving systems adopted fast. You attach no probabilities. That honesty matters.

What the post softens is the distribution. In substantial, labor’s share of income slips from about 60% to 56.1% and knowledge-worker wages are roughly flat. In extreme, labor’s share falls to 45.2%, cognitive wages are more than 10% below the no-AI path, cognitive unemployment is modeled near 18%, and economy-wide unemployment near 12%. Growth in every scenario is not the same as shared gains. Capital takes the residual.

Two limits should sit next to the explorer. The write-up sets aside business cycles, policy response, catastrophic risk, and hyper-capable robots. A US-only task model to 2030 cannot speak to global diffusion, energy and compute constraints, or an alignment failure if RSI arrives inside that window. The same week, your alignment lead put a personal figure above 10% on human-level catastrophe this decade and said there is not yet a plan to align superintelligence. Those statements live in a different column from +32% GDP.

So: use the explorer as a map of task substitution and factor shares. Do not read “the economy grows in all three scenarios” as a welfare result, and do not treat the extreme case as both an economic boom and a safety non-event. The useful public question is which scenario you are steering toward, and which instruments, if any, decide who captures the increment.
